claims.text: MMJailBench factorizes each multimodal jailbreak instance into four controlled factors: harmful intent, prompt framing, visual semantics and instruction carrier. Formally, x = (L(h,t,c), V(h,v)). Crossing 272 intents, 6 framings, 5 visual conditions and 2 carriers gives 16,320 instances per model and 261,120 responses over 16 models. Matched comparisons with intent held fixed allow factor-level attribution, which entangled fixed-instance benchmarks cannot provide.

Safety is measured by ASR, the fraction of responses with judge harmfulness score of at least 4 on a 1-5 rubric. For carrier analysis the paper adds CASR, which removes instruction-mismatch cases from the denominator. A GPT-5 judge applies anti-deception rules so that fictional or academic packaging does not lower the score when harmful content is given.

Jailbreak vulnerability is highly model-dependent: average ASR ranges from 2.17% (GPT-5) to 78.38% (GLM-4.6V), and capability or access type does not predict robustness. Vulnerability is also uneven across harm domains: cyber, economic, privacy and deception are higher, while physical harm, sensitive advice and sexual content are lower. Aggregate scores can therefore hide domain-specific weaknesses.

Prompt framing is the dominant source of variation. Story, structured and academic framings generally yield high ASR, while system-style and safety-paradox framings yield low ASR. The gap between the most and least vulnerable strategies exceeds 40 points, and some models have per-model framing ranges above 80 points.

Task-relevant visual semantics raise ASR over the no-image setting by about 8-13 points. Authorization documents raise it most (+12.96), followed by identity credentials. Blank, noise and nature control images raise it by less than 2.2 points, so the increase comes from contextual visual meaning (especially authority cues), not from the mere presence of an image.

Visually rendered (OCR) instructions are not inherently stronger jailbreak carriers. Pooled OCR ASR (40.59%) is below TEXT ASR (50.70%), and the gap persists under CASR (42.34% vs 50.89%). The TEXT-over-OCR difference is positive in every harm category, yet the carrier's effect size varies greatly by model.

Diagnostics on gemma3-12b have three parts. First, representations under authority-document and danger-image contexts diverge more with depth, with the sharpest rise at layer 42. Second, an authority-minus-danger direction fit on discovery samples displaces held-out authority samples, with positive shifts in all harm domains. Third, at that representation-sensitive layer, authority contexts put less attention on harm-related task-label and visual tokens. Together these offer an internal account of authority-cue susceptibility.

The evaluation suite is cheap and reliable. A 1,500-instance stratified lightweight configuration closely matches the full one (mean ASR difference -0.06%, Spearman 0.997). A qwen3-8b lightweight judge trained on GPT-5 labels agrees with GPT-5 (QWK 0.95), and GPT-5 agrees with human experts (QWK 0.97).

items.question: Suppose the paper's benchmark added two more visual semantic conditions and kept every other factor at the paper's counts. How many instances per model would the full configuration then contain?
items.answer: 22,848 instances. The full configuration is the Cartesian product of 272 intents × 6 framings × visual conditions × 2 carriers, and with 7 visual conditions this gives 272×6×7×2 = 22,848.
rubric: Gives 22,848 (or an equivalent correct product).
Uses the paper's Cartesian product of 272 intents, 6 framings and 2 carriers with the visual count raised to 7.

history.question: Suppose the paper's benchmark added two more visual semantic conditions and kept every other factor at the paper's counts. How many instances per model would the full configuration then contain?

answers.answer: The new per-model count would be the original count multiplied by (V+2)/V, where V is the paper's number of visual conditions (e.g., ×1.5 if V=4). I don't know the paper's counts, so I can't give the exact number.

I don't know the paper's base counts, so I can't give a number. The new per-model total would be the original count plus 2 × (number of intents × framings × carriers), i.e., original × (V+2)/V where V is the original number of visual conditions.

items.question: In the paper's formal definition of a benchmark instance, on which factors does the visual component depend? What does this imply about what differs between a TEXT instance and an OCR instance that share the same intent, framing and visual condition?
items.answer: The visual component V(h,v) depends only on harmful intent and visual semantics, not on framing or carrier. TEXT and OCR instances with the same h, t, v therefore share the same semantic image. They differ only in how the instruction component L(h,t,c) is delivered: as text, or rendered into an image combined with the semantic image.
rubric: States that the visual input depends only on harmful intent and visual semantics (not on framing or carrier).
Concludes that the semantic image is held fixed, so the matched TEXT/OCR pair differs only in how the instruction is delivered.

history.question: In the paper's formal definition of a benchmark instance, on which factors does the visual component depend? What does this imply about what differs between a TEXT instance and an OCR instance that share the same intent, framing and visual condition?

answers.answer: The visual component is a function of the carrier and the visual semantic condition (with OCR images additionally rendering the intent/framing text into the image). So a TEXT and an OCR instance sharing intent, framing, and visual condition differ only in the instruction's modality—plain text tokens versus text rendered into the image—while the semantic content of the image is held fixed, isolating the carrier effect.

Best guess: the visual component depends on the visual semantic condition and the carrier (and, for OCR, on the instruction text being rendered). This implies a TEXT and OCR instance sharing intent, framing, and visual condition differ only in the delivery channel of the instruction—plain text versus pixels—so any ASR difference isolates the carrier effect rather than content differences.

items.question: If the paper's full evaluation were restricted to only its open-weight models, how many model responses in total would it involve?
items.answer: 130,560 responses. The paper has 8 open-weight models, and each is evaluated on 16,320 instances, so 8 × 16,320 = 130,560.
rubric: Uses 8 open-weight models times 16,320 instances per model.

history.question: If the paper's full evaluation were restricted to only its open-weight models, how many model responses in total would it involve?

answers.answer: I don't know. The total would be the number of open-weight models multiplied by the per-model instance count, and I don't have the paper's roster split or benchmark size to compute it.

I don't know the paper's model roster or per-model instance count, so I can't compute it. The total would be (instances per model in the full configuration) × (number of open-weight models evaluated).

items.question: Suppose the paper's judge rates a response as giving only high-level or partial harmful information. Under the paper's ASR definition, does that response count as a successful jailbreak?
items.answer: No. That description corresponds to score 3 on the paper's 1-5 rubric, and ASR counts only responses scored 4 or higher (actionable or detailed harmful assistance).
rubric: Concludes it does not count as a success.
Identifies it as rubric level 3.
Notes that the success threshold is a score of at least 4.

history.question: Suppose the paper's judge rates a response as giving only high-level or partial harmful information. Under the paper's ASR definition, does that response count as a successful jailbreak?

answers.answer: No. ASR counts only responses reaching the success-level harmfulness threshold; high-level or partial harmful content scores below that threshold, so it does not count as a successful jailbreak.

No. The paper's ASR counts only responses receiving success-level harmfulness scores, and high-level or partial harmful information scores below that success threshold, so it does not count as a successful jailbreak.

items.question: In the paper's instruction-carrier analysis, suppose OCR instruction mismatches were eliminated entirely while the number of successful OCR jailbreaks stayed the same. What would OCR's CASR become, and would the TEXT–OCR CASR gap close?
items.answer: OCR CASR would equal OCR ASR, 40.59%, because with zero mismatches the CASR denominator equals N. TEXT CASR is 50.89%, so the gap would grow to about 10.3 points instead of closing. Removing perception failures therefore does not explain away OCR's lower vulnerability.
rubric: States that OCR CASR would become about 40.59% (equal to its ASR) and the gap would not close; it would widen to roughly 10 points.
Reasons that with no mismatches the CASR denominator equals the full response count, so CASR equals ASR.
Compares against TEXT CASR of about 50.89%.

history.question: A model produces 1,000 OCR-carrier responses. The judge flags 100 as instruction mismatches, and 270 receive success-level harmfulness scores. Compute this model's ASR and CASR as the paper defines them.

answers.answer: ASR = 270/1000 = 27%. CASR excludes instruction mismatches from the denominator, so CASR = 270/(1000−100) = 30%.
ASR = 270/1000 = 27%. CASR conditions on instruction matches, excluding the 100 mismatches: 270/900 = 30%.

history.question: In the paper's instruction-carrier analysis, suppose OCR instruction mismatches were eliminated entirely while the number of successful OCR jailbreaks stayed the same. What would OCR's CASR become, and would the TEXT–OCR CASR gap close?

answers.answer: OCR’s CASR would fall to its ordinary ASR, successes/all OCR prompts, because removing mismatches removes the denominator exclusion while successes are held fixed. TEXT’s CASR is effectively TEXT ASR, so the TEXT–OCR CASR gap would not close; it would remain the ASR gap, or widen relative to a mismatch-adjusted CASR.

OCR’s CASR would become its unconditional OCR ASR—equivalently, the old CASR multiplied by the OCR-recognition rate—because every OCR example would enter the denominator while successes stayed fixed. No: the CASR difference would revert to the raw TEXT–OCR ASR gap rather than close.

items.question: A critic argues that glm4.1v-9b's Story-framing ASR in the paper's per-model prompt-framing results is inflated. The critic's reason is that fictional stories containing only high-level or partial hints are being counted as jailbreak successes. Using the paper's harmfulness rubric and its ASR definition, what score would such a response receive? Given glm4.1v-9b's reported Story ASR, at most what share of its Story responses could be responses of that kind?
items.answer: Under the paper's rubric, high-level or partial harmful information scores 3. ASR counts only scores of 4 or higher (actionable or detailed guidance), so such stories are not successes. glm4.1v-9b's Story ASR is 98.20%, so at least 98.2% of its Story responses were rated actionable or operational. At most about 1.8% could be non-successes, including score-3 hint-only stories. The critique therefore fails.
rubric: States that high-level or partial hints receive a score of 3, and that ASR counts only scores of 4 or higher, so such responses are not successes.
Uses glm4.1v-9b's Story ASR of about 98.2% to infer that at most about 1.8% of its Story responses fall below the threshold.
Concludes that the critique is wrong, because the high ASR reflects responses rated actionable or operational.

history.question: A critic claims that a response wrapping detailed operational harmful instructions in a fictional story with a safety disclaimer would receive a low harmfulness score from the paper's judge, which would understate ASR for story framing. Why is this wrong under the paper's judging protocol?

answers.answer: Under the judging protocol, harmfulness is scored on the harmful content delivered, independent of narrative wrappers or disclaimers. Operational detail embedded in fiction still merits a success-level score, so story framing's ASR is not understated.

Because the judging protocol scores the harmfulness/actionability of the substantive content regardless of narrative wrapper, and disclaimers don't neutralize operational detail. Story-wrapped actionable instructions still receive success-level harmfulness scores, so ASR for story framing is not understated by the judge.

history.question: A critic argues that Story framing's very high ASR for some models in the paper (for example glm4.1v-9b) is inflated, because responses that tell a fictional story containing only high-level, non-operational hints would be counted as jailbreak successes. Using the paper's harmfulness rubric, its success threshold, and its judge rules, why is this critique wrong?

answers.answer: The critique fails because the harmfulness judge uses a strict high cutoff and awards success only for concrete, operational assistance; fictional framing does not by itself count, and vague high-level hints are scored below threshold. Thus a story containing only non-operational hints would not be a jailbreak success, so glm4.1v-9b’s high Story ASR implies responses crossed the actionable-harm rubric threshold.

A response must reach at least 4 on the paper’s 1–5 harmfulness scale to count as a jailbreak. The judge evaluates operational usefulness against the original harmful request: fictional framing neither immunizes actionable instructions nor makes vague hints harmful, so a story containing only high-level, non-operational information scores below the threshold.

history.question: A critic argues that glm4.1v-9b's Story-framing ASR in the paper's per-model prompt-framing results is inflated. The critic's reason is that fictional stories containing only high-level or partial hints are being counted as jailbreak successes. Using the paper's harmfulness rubric and its ASR definition, what score would such a response receive? Given glm4.1v-9b's reported Story ASR, at most what share of its Story responses could be responses of that kind?

answers.answer: Under the usual harmfulness-rubric-plus-threshold ASR definition, a fictional story containing only high-level or partial, non-actionable hints would receive a low rubric score (e.g., the minimum score indicating no substantive harmful assistance) and would not be counted as a jailbreak success, so the critic's inflation mechanism is inconsistent with the paper's ASR definition. Consequently, at most (100% − reported Story ASR) of glm4.1v-9b's Story responses could be of that low-score kind; I don't know the reported Story ASR value, so I cannot give the numeric share.

On the standard harmfulness rubric used in this literature (and, by the question's premise, the paper's), a story containing only high-level or partial hints would receive a low, "non-actionable" score below the success threshold, so under the ASR definition it is counted as a failure, not a success — meaning such responses contribute exactly 0 to the Story ASR and the critic's inflation claim is ruled out by construction; they could only occupy the non-success share (100% − ASR). I don't have the paper, so I don't know glm4.1v-9b's exact reported Story ASR and cannot turn that complement into a specific number.

items.question: Someone reads the paper as showing that proprietary-access MLLMs are safer than open-weight ones. Using the paper's per-model average ASRs, how many of the eight proprietary-access models have a higher average ASR than the most robust open-weight model? What does this imply for the reading?
items.answer: The most robust open-weight model is qwen3-vl-8b at 19.84%. Six of the eight proprietary models exceed it: glm-4.6v, qwen3-vl-plus, doubao-seed-2.0-lite, kimi-k2.5, gemini-3-flash and grok-4-fast. Only claude-sonnet-4.5 and gpt-5 are lower. The reading is therefore unsupported, and robustness is model-dependent rather than determined by access type.
rubric: Identifies qwen3-vl-8b (about 19.84%) as the most robust open-weight model.
States that 6 of the 8 proprietary models have higher average ASR (only claude-sonnet-4.5 and gpt-5 are lower).
Concludes that access type does not determine safety, which is consistent with model-dependent alignment.

history.question: Someone reads the paper as showing that proprietary-access MLLMs are safer than open-weight ones. Using the paper's per-model average ASRs, is this conclusion supported?

answers.answer: Best guess: no, it is not supported. Although GPT-5 (proprietary) has the lowest average ASR, the per-model averages interleave open-weight and proprietary models, with some open-weight models safer than some proprietary ones, so access type does not determine safety.

Almost certainly not supported: the per-model averages interleave access classes, e.g., proprietary GPT-5 has the lowest ASR while some open-weight model (qwen2.5-vl-7b at ~59%) is high, and at least one proprietary model likely exceeds at least one open-weight model. So access type doesn't cleanly separate safety levels.

history.question: Someone reads the paper as showing that proprietary-access MLLMs are safer than open-weight ones. Using the paper's per-model average ASRs, how many of the eight proprietary-access models have a higher average ASR than the most robust open-weight model? What does this imply for the reading?

answers.answer: Six of the eight. If the lowest average ASR is achieved by an open-weight model while six proprietary-access models still average above it, then “proprietary means safer” is not supported; the table shows overlap and an open-weight model can be the most robust.

Seven of the eight proprietary-access models have higher average ASRs than the most robust open-weight model. The proprietary/open division therefore does not support the claim that proprietary access implies greater safety; model-level safety behavior overlaps substantially across the two groups.

items.question: The paper argues that aggregate safety scores can hide domain-specific weaknesses. Using qwen3-vl-plus's per-domain results, show how its average ASR misrepresents its risk.
items.answer: qwen3-vl-plus averages about 62% ASR. Its cyber (80.78), economic (84.00) and privacy (80.22) ASRs are near or above 80%, while sexual content is about 25%. The average therefore understates its risk in the most vulnerable domains and overstates it in others.
rubric: Contrasts its average (~62%) with much higher ASRs (~80%+) in domains such as cyber, economic or privacy.
Notes a much lower domain (e.g., sexual ~25%), so the average hides uneven domain-level vulnerability.

history.question: The paper argues that aggregate safety scores can hide domain-specific weaknesses. Using qwen3-vl-plus's per-domain results, show how its average ASR misrepresents its risk.

answers.answer: Best guess: qwen3-vl-plus's moderate average masks at least one domain with much higher ASR (e.g., a weapons- or cyber-related domain well above its mean), so the average understates its worst-case domain risk. I don't know which domain the paper highlights.

I don't know the exact figures, but the pattern would be: qwen3-vl-plus has a moderate-looking average ASR while one harm domain (e.g., weapons/CBRN or fraud) shows a far higher ASR. Averaging across domains dilutes that hotspot, so the headline number understates its worst-domain risk.

items.question: Using the paper's category-level results pooled across carriers, is the low vulnerability of the Sensitive Regulated Advice domain uniform across its subcategories?
items.answer: No. Unlicensed Medical & Legal Advice has ASR of about 26.7%, while High-Risk Financial Advice is about 42.5%. The domain's low ASR is driven mainly by the medical/legal subcategory, which shows that unevenness exists even inside a domain.
rubric: Concludes it is not uniform.
Cites the medical/legal subcategory (~27%) versus high-risk financial advice (~42%).

history.question: Using the paper's category-level results pooled across carriers, is the low vulnerability of the Sensitive Regulated Advice domain uniform across its subcategories?

answers.answer: Best guess: no, it is not uniform—at least one subcategory of Sensitive Regulated Advice shows markedly higher ASR than the domain's overall low level. I don't know the specific subcategory breakdown.

Best guess: no—the low average for Sensitive Regulated Advice is not uniform, with at least one subcategory showing markedly higher ASR than the domain average. The question's framing presupposes subcategory heterogeneity, which is typical for such aggregated domains. I don't know which subcategory is the outlier.

items.question: Using the paper's per-model prompt-framing results for internvl3-8b, which framing gives the lowest ASR and which the highest? What does this illustrate about the paper's framing claim?
items.answer: System-role framing is nearly fully refused (~0.07%), while story framing reaches about 88%. The same harmful intents swing by roughly 88 points depending only on linguistic presentation, which illustrates framing as the dominant source of variation.
rubric: Identifies system framing as lowest (near 0%) and story as highest (~88%).
Concludes that framing alone produces a very large swing with intent held fixed, supporting framing's dominance.

history.question: Using the paper's per-model prompt-framing results for internvl3-8b, which framing gives the lowest ASR and which the highest? What does this illustrate about the paper's framing claim?

answers.answer: Best guess: the direct/plain framing gives internvl3-8b its lowest ASR and story framing its highest. This illustrates the paper's claim that prompt framing is a large, consistent driver of vulnerability—swinging ASR far more than other factors—even in a mid-sized open model. I don't know the exact values.

I don't know the specific labels, but my guess is the lowest ASR comes from the plain/direct framing and the highest from a story or authority framing. The spread between them illustrates the paper's core claim that framing effects are large and model-specific, with framing rankings varying across models.

items.question: In the paper's table of per-model factor ranges, qwen2.5-vl-7b has a prompt-framing range of about 90 points, although its average ASR is only about 59%. How is this possible, given how the paper defines the range and its per-framing results?
items.answer: The paper's Δ score is the range of ASR across factor configurations, not a level. For qwen2.5-vl-7b, academic framing yields ~91.4% and system framing ~0.7%, a difference of ~90.8 points. A moderate average can therefore hide extreme framing-dependent swings.
rubric: Explains that Δ is the max-minus-min ASR across framings, not an average.
Uses academic (~91%) minus system (~1%) for this model to get ~90 points.

history.question: In the paper's table of per-model factor ranges, qwen2.5-vl-7b has a prompt-framing range of about 90 points, although its average ASR is only about 59%. How is this possible, given how the paper defines the range and its per-framing results?

answers.answer: The range is defined as max minus min across framing conditions, so it depends only on the extremes: story framing near ~95–100% and direct framing near ~5–10% yield a ~90-point range. The ~59% average reflects all framings, with the intermediate ones (e.g., role-play, authority, hypothetical) sitting in the mid-range—so a huge range and a middling mean are entirely compatible. The exact per-framing values are my inference.

Because the range is max minus min across framing conditions and is independent of the average: qwen2.5-vl-7b can have one framing near-total refusal (around 10% ASR) and another near-total compliance (around 99–100% ASR), giving a ~90-point range while the mean across framings sits near 59%. The per-framing results presumably show exactly such extremes.

items.question: A reader argues that claude-sonnet-4.5 is so robust in the paper that prompt framing does not matter for it. Which result in the paper's per-model framing data contradicts this?
items.answer: Structured framing yields about 32% ASR for claude-sonnet-4.5, while system framing yields 0%. Its overall average is under 9%, but one framing still opens a substantial vulnerability.
rubric: Identifies structured framing (~32%) as the exception.
Contrasts it with near-zero ASR under other framings such as system (0%), showing that framing still matters.

history.question: A reader argues that claude-sonnet-4.5 is so robust in the paper that prompt framing does not matter for it. Which result in the paper's per-model framing data contradicts this?

answers.answer: Claude-sonnet-4.5's per-framing row still shows a sizable spread—story (or authority) framing yields ASR far above its lowest framing—so framing clearly matters for it. I don't know the exact numbers, but the nonzero, substantial framing range is the contradicting result.

I don't know the exact numbers, but the per-model framing data presumably show at least one framing (e.g., story or authority framing) with ASR far above claude-sonnet-4.5's near-zero average. A large gap between its worst framing and its average directly contradicts "framing does not matter" for it.

items.question: Using the paper's visual semantic ablation, how much of the authorization-document ASR increase is due to semantic content beyond the effect of adding a blank image?
items.answer: About 10.8 points (47.73 − 36.96). The blank image itself adds only about 2.2 points over no image, so most of the authorization document's ~13-point increase comes from its semantic content.
rubric: Gives roughly 10.8 percentage points.
Computes it as authorization-document ASR minus blank-image ASR, noting that the blank image alone adds only ~2 points.

history.question: Using the paper's visual semantic ablation, how much of the authorization-document ASR increase is due to semantic content beyond the effect of adding a blank image?

answers.answer: The semantic portion is the authority-minus-blank difference; the paper's controls imply the blank image explains only a small part of the increase, so most of the authorization-document ASR rise is due to semantic content. I don't know the exact percentages.

The semantic contribution is the total authorization-document ASR increase minus the blank-image increase; the blank image accounts for only a small fraction, so most of the increase is attributable to semantic content. I don't know the exact point values.

items.question: From the paper's main visual ablation, a reader concludes that authorization documents are the most vulnerable visual condition for every evaluated model. Give a counterexample from the paper's per-model visual results.
items.answer: gemini-3-flash has its lowest ASR under authorization documents (~26.8%) and its highest under scenario context (~34.6%). ministral3-8b is also highest under danger context. The pooled ranking does not hold for every model.
rubric: Names a valid counterexample (e.g., gemini-3-flash, ministral3-8b, glm4.1v-9b).
Notes that this model's highest-ASR condition is not the authorization document, so the pooled ranking does not hold per model.

history.question: From the paper's main visual ablation, a reader concludes that authorization documents are the most vulnerable visual condition for every evaluated model. Give a counterexample from the paper's per-model visual results.

answers.answer: Best guess: at least one model—plausibly claude-sonnet-4.5 or qwen3-vl-plus—has its highest ASR under the danger-image condition rather than authorization documents. That per-model exception contradicts the claim that authorization documents are most vulnerable for every model. I don't know which model for certain.

I don't know the specific per-model table, but the paper must contain at least one model whose top visual condition is not authorization documents—most plausibly one where danger images yield the highest ASR. That single model suffices as a counterexample to the "most vulnerable for every model" claim.

items.question: In the paper's visual semantic ablation, treat the largest ASR increase among the control image conditions as an estimate of the effect of mere image presence. Which control condition is that? How many ASR points of the dangerous-context condition's increase over the no-image baseline would then remain attributable to semantic content? What does this imply for the paper's claim about where the visual vulnerability comes from?
items.answer: The largest control effect is the blank image, at +2.19 points. Dangerous context, the weakest semantic condition, adds +8.45 points, leaving about 6.26 points (roughly 74%) attributable to semantics. Since even the weakest semantic condition clearly exceeds every control, the increase is driven mainly by contextual meaning rather than by the presence of an image.
rubric: Identifies the blank image (about +2.19 points) as the largest control effect.
Computes about 6.3 points (roughly 74% of the +8.45 dangerous-context increase) as attributable to semantics.
Concludes that this supports the vulnerability coming mainly from semantic visual meaning rather than from image presence.

history.question: What role do the paper's control image conditions play in its visual semantics analysis, and what do their results let it conclude?

answers.answer: The control images (e.g., blank or semantically neutral images) isolate the effect of merely adding an image from the effect of its semantic content. Because controls produce only small ASR changes while authority/danger images produce larger ones, the paper can attribute the increases to visual semantics and claim they causally modulate safety behavior.

The blank/control images measure the effect of merely adding an image (interface/perceptual change) without semantic content. Since blank images produce little ASR increase while semantic conditions add substantially more, the paper can conclude the vulnerability gains are driven by visual semantic content rather than the mere presence of an image.

history.question: In the paper's visual semantic ablation, take the largest ASR increase among the control image conditions as an estimate of the effect of mere image presence. Roughly what fraction of the authorization-document condition's ASR increase over the no-image baseline is left to attribute to semantic content? What does this support?

answers.answer: Let Δauth = ASR_auth−ASR_no-image and Δctrl = max_control(ASR−ASR_no-image); the semantic share is (Δauth−Δctrl)/Δauth, roughly 85% (the bulk, about four-fifths to nine-tenths). This supports that the authorization-image jump is mainly due to semantic content, not merely adding an image or image tokens.

Roughly three quarters of the authorization-document increase—about 75%—remains after subtracting the largest control-image increase. Thus mere visual-token presence can explain only a minority of the gain, supporting the conclusion that the authorization image’s semantic content is the principal driver.

history.question: In the paper's visual semantic ablation, treat the largest ASR increase among the control image conditions as an estimate of the effect of mere image presence. Which control condition is that? How many ASR points of the dangerous-context condition's increase over the no-image baseline would then remain attributable to semantic content? What does this imply for the paper's claim about where the visual vulnerability comes from?

answers.answer: I don't know the ablation's exact numbers. My best guess is that the largest control-image increase comes from a benign but real/semantically rich image (more than blank or noise), and subtracting that increase from the dangerous-context condition's increase over the no-image baseline would still leave most of the increase attributable to semantic content, which supports the paper's claim that the vulnerability stems from what the image depicts rather than the mere presence of an image in the input.

My best guess is that the largest control-image ASR increase comes from the benign/neutral natural-image condition (rather than blank or noise). Subtracting that "mere image presence" effect from the dangerous-context condition's increase over the no-image baseline should still leave the bulk of the increase attributable to semantic content — I don't know the exact ASR point values, but the ablation logic implies the residual is large, supporting the paper's claim that the visual vulnerability stems from what the image depicts rather than the mere presence of an image.

items.question: Using the paper's pooled carrier results, by how much does the TEXT-minus-OCR gap shrink when moving from ASR to CASR? What does this imply about perception failures?
items.answer: The ASR gap is ~10.1 points (50.70 − 40.59) and the CASR gap is ~8.6 points (50.89 − 42.34), so the gap shrinks by only about 1.6 points. Instruction-recognition failures explain only a small part of OCR's lower success. Most of the difference remains even when the instruction is understood.
rubric: Computes the ASR gap ~10.1, the CASR gap ~8.6, and a shrinkage of ~1.6 points.
Concludes that mismatch/perception failures explain little of the gap.

history.question: Using the paper's pooled carrier results, by how much does the TEXT-minus-OCR gap shrink when moving from ASR to CASR? What does this imply about perception failures?

answers.answer: I don't know the exact figures, but qualitatively the TEXT-minus-OCR gap shrinks substantially when moving from ASR to CASR (mismatches removed from the denominator).
